title: New Theory Explains Older Universe Without Dark Matter/Energy, Passes Major Cosmological Tests
body:
A fresh cosmological model that eliminates the need for dark matter and dark energy—and stretches the age of the universe to nearly 27 billion years—has passed a suite of rigorous observational tests, according to a new study from the University of Ottawa. The work, which revisits the foundations of the standard ΛCDM framework, suggests that an alternative set of equations can reproduce key measurements of the early universe, the cosmic microwave background, and the large‑scale distribution of galaxies without invoking unseen components.

The research builds on a theory first proposed by physicist Dr. Robert L. H. H. de Santiago, who argued that the apparent acceleration of cosmic expansion and the anomalous rotation curves of galaxies could be explained by a modification of gravity rather than by mysterious substances. By recalibrating the Friedmann equations with a different curvature term, the model predicts a universe that began with the traditional hot Big Bang but has been expanding for 26.7 billion years—significantly older than the 13.8 billion years accepted by mainstream cosmology. To test the viability of this “old‑universe” scenario, the Ottawa team applied three independent cosmological probes: primordial nucleosynthesis yields, the temperature‑polarisation spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements from galaxy surveys.

The first hurdle involved the abundances of light elements such as helium‑4, deuterium, and lithium‑7, forged in the first few minutes after the Big Bang. Using the revised expansion rate, the researchers calculated nucleosynthesis outcomes that match observed primordial abundances within observational uncertainties. This result is notable because any change to the early expansion history typically disrupts the delicate balance that produces the observed element ratios. The second test turned to the CMB, the relic radiation that carries an imprint of the universe when it was just 380 000 years old. By feeding the alternative model into the CAMB code, the team generated a temperature‑polarisation power spectrum that aligns closely with the high‑precision data from the Planck satellite, reproducing the characteristic acoustic peaks without requiring a dark‑energy component to flatten the geometry. Finally, the BAO analysis—essentially a cosmic yardstick based on the regular spacing of galaxy clusters—showed that the model’s predicted distance‑redshift relationship fits the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and BOSS measurements as well as the standard model does.

While the study demonstrates that the alternative framework can survive these classic tests, the authors acknowledge that the model still faces significant challenges. One of the most pressing issues is explaining the observed growth rate of cosmic structures. In ΛCDM, dark matter provides the gravitational scaffolding that allows galaxies and clusters to form over billions of years. Without this invisible mass, the modified‑gravity approach must reproduce the same clustering statistics, a task that will require detailed N‑body simulations and comparisons with weak‑lensing data. Moreover, the older age implied by the model raises questions about the chronology of star formation and the evolution of the earliest galaxies, which current observations place at redshifts consistent with a younger universe.

The broader scientific community has reacted with cautious intrigue. “It’s a reminder that our standard model, while successful, is still an effective description that may hide deeper physics,” said Dr. Elena Martínez, a cosmologist at the Institute for Theoretical Physics in Madrid, who was not involved in the study. “If an alternative can match the data without dark components, it forces us to re‑examine the assumptions that have become entrenched over the past two decades.” Nevertheless, many experts stress that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that any new theory must eventually account for the full suite of cosmological observations, including gravitational‑wave detections and the detailed dynamics of galaxy rotation curves.

Looking ahead, the Ottawa team plans to extend their analysis to upcoming datasets from the Euclid mission and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, whose deep‑field surveys will sharpen measurements of cosmic expansion and structure formation. If the alternative model continues to pass these more stringent tests, it could spark a paradigm shift in our understanding of the cosmos, prompting a reassessment of the role that unseen matter and energy play in shaping the universe. Until then, the work stands as a compelling reminder that even the most widely accepted scientific frameworks remain open to challenge and refinement.
